somalia.title: Militants kill 20 soldiers in ambush in Somalia - Taipei Times
somalia.content: Militants kill 20 soldiers in ambush in Somalia - Taipei Times Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News Thu, Oct 29, 2026 page5 Militants kill 20 soldiers in ambush in Somalia AP, MOGADISHU Add TT as Preferred Source Militants killed at least 20 Somalian soldiers in an ambush, a military officer who survived the attack said, as the government acknowledged damage to military vehicles, but disclosed no troop casualties. The al-Shabaab group, which has fought Somalia’s government for nearly two decades, claimed responsibility for Monday’s attack near Jameeca village in southern Somalia. The Somalian Ministry of Defence said that its troops killed about 75 militants and wounded 56 during hours of fighting. Al-Shabaab fighters hold weapons as they conduct military exercises in Mogadishu on Oct. 21, 2010. Photo: AP Al-Shabaab said that it killed 321 soldiers, and captured prisoners and military equipment. The casualty figures and claims of captured soldiers and equipment could not be independently verified. Abshir Abdikarim, a military officer traveling with the convoy, told reporters by phone late on Tuesday that he saw at least 20 of his fellow soldiers dead after the attack. Troops had advanced from Leego into Jameeca, in Burhakaba district in the Bay region, where they exchanged heavy gunfire with militants, he said. Some soldiers previously reported missing reached Baledogle on Tuesday, he said, while others remained unaccounted for. The ministry described the confrontation as an assault on militant positions. Al-Shabaab said its fighters ambushed a convoy advancing into territory under its control. The ministry said militants used explosives-laden vehicles to attack army vehicles, damaging some of them. It did not specify how many were damaged or address the claims that soldiers had been captured. Al-Shabaab said it seized Turkish-supplied armored vehicles, armed pickup trucks, supply trucks, weapons and ammunition. African Union troops pushed al-Shabaab out of Mogadishu in 2011, but the group adapted through guerrilla warfare, suicide bombings and targeted assassinations. Somalian authorities have reported territorial gains during a US-backed military campaign, although access restrictions have made those claims difficult to verify independently. The militants have retained the ability to operate across large areas of central and southern Somalia. The fighting comes amid a separate struggle for control of South West state. somalia.title: Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 - IFA - Institute of Foreign Affairs
somalia.content: Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 - IFA Contact Us English Subscribe Topics Regions Events Publications Academy Media About Us ← Back to Blog Policy Briefs • 13 min read • October 28, 2026 Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 Executive Summary Ethiopia's security interest in Somalia is best protected by working through Mogadishu, the African Union (AU) and the Ankara process, while strengthening its own border security and assessing its maritime exposure before signing new agreements. The decisive date is 31 December 2026. The United States told the AU on 1 July 2026 that it will not fund UN logistics for the AU Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) beyond that date, and the mission's mandate expires then. The period leading to this deadline warrants sustained diplomatic and security attention. Somalia's deterioration predates the 2024 political disputes. The offensive against Al-Shabaab lost momentum by mid-2023 because of funding gaps, the drawdown of the earlier AU mission (ATMIS), constraints on Somali National Army logistics and reduced operational capacity among clan militias. The federal–member-state dispute aggravated the decline but did not originate it. Two threats need separate treatment: Al-Shabaab in south-central Somalia, and piracy, renewed since April 2026 and centered on the Puntland coast. Open sources show no operational link between them. Ethiopia's clearest exposure is on land, where Al-Shabaab's July 2022 incursion into the Somali Region is the precedent; its maritime exposure is smaller and indirect. Ethiopia should engage the federal and member states authorities as complementary partners within the framework of AU principles and give priority to a post-2026 AUSSOM agreement, border defence with the Somali regional state and a maritime risk assessment. 1. Background: the Ankara baseline The Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024 reset relations after the Ethiopia-Somaliland memorandum of understanding (MoU) of 1 January 2024. Under Turkish mediation, Somalia lifted its objection to Ethiopian participation in AUSSOM, and both governments committed to respect sovereignty while negotiating commercial arrangements for Ethiopian sea access. ¹ In September 2026 Somalia said the declaration remains the governing framework. ² Three matters stay open. The Somaliland MoU is unresolved rather than operative; in October 2026 Somaliland said it was ready to discuss Ethiopian access to Berbera, without terms. ³ Sea-access talks have reportedly made little progress, a claim to be checked against Ethiopian official statements. ⁴ And most Ethiopian troops serve bilaterally rather than under AUSSOM, which began operating in January 2025.⁵ 2. Why Somalia's security deteriorated The federal–member-state dispute weakened a campaign that was already stalling. A clan-militia-backed offensive retook territory in 2022, but Phase Two was postponed in June 2023, before the MoU and the March 2024 constitutional amendments. ⁶ Al-Shabaab's 2025 counteroffensive was timed to the end of the ATMIS drawdown. ⁷ The March 2026 amendments, which extended terms from four to five years and were rejected by Puntland and Jubaland, escalated the dispute only after the main territorial losses. ⁸ 3. Two separate threats Al-Shabaab: persistent security threat. The group reversed most 2022–23 gains in 2025 but stalled in the second half of the year, so the threat is entrenchment in the south-centre, rather than evidence of an imminent advance on Mogadishu. Its push toward Lower Shabelle met resistance from Somali forces backed by AU troops and US and Turkish airpower. ¹³ The dispute now has a military edge in the south-west: federal troops sent to Baidoa in March 2026 were ambushed in May, and Southwest State, which borders Ethiopia, suspended cooperation with Mogadishu. ¹⁴ Political and military risk overlap most for Addis Ababa here. The 2026 evidence is thinner and should be refreshed against UN Panel of Experts and ACLED data. Piracy: A Separate Maritime Front. Six commercial vessels were hijacked between 21 April and 22 August 2026, most recently the tanker Sibu 1; Somali pirates accounted for 94% of hostages taken worldwide in the first half of 2026. ¹⁵ Puntland says forces beyond its control are responsible; sources do not name them, so this brief makes no attribution. Puntland has fought ISIS-Somalia in the Cal Miskaad mountains since December 2024, which shapes its coastal force posture. ¹⁶ No evidence links the hijackings to Al-Shabaab, so earlier "safe haven" claims are dropped. 4. Implications for Ethiopia The documented risk is a repeat of 20 July 2022, when Al-Shabaab attacked Liyu police posts in Bakool and crossed into the Somali Region, its biggest operation inside Ethiopia according to VOA. ¹⁷ Estimates of the force range from about 250 to 500 fighters. ¹⁸ Three conditions enabled it: Al-Shabaab control of Bakool and Gedo border areas, thin Ethiopian presence on the border, and forces committed elsewhere during the Tigray war. These are the indicators to watch. Al-Shabaab has not claimed attacks in Ethiopia since mid-2022, so a repeat is credible but not demonstrated. ¹⁹ Egypt and Somalia signed a defence agreement in August 2024, and a contingent of just over 1,000 is due to join AUSSOM; Somalia attributes the delay to funding and logistics.²⁰ The sources reviewed do not establish an intention by Egypt to contribute to instability in Somalia, though analysts warn Somalia could become a proxy theatre if tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia escalate. ²¹ A practical priority is ensuring coordination and avoiding operational misunderstandings wherever forces are deployed. Turkey brokered the Ankara Declaration and has maintained diplomatic engagement with both capitals, making it central to any sea-access or AUSSOM compromise. In January 2026 Mogadishu cancelled all UAE agreements, including port deals at Berbera, Bossaso and Kismayo, after Israel recognized Somaliland; Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland rejected the decision. ²² Ethiopia's Berbera interest and the federal dispute both run through this relationship. Djibouti carried 96.71% of Ethiopia's external freight in fiscal 2025/26, and Berbera 2.74% of the 15.34 million tons on maritime corridors. ²³ Exposure is therefore indirect: ships serving both ports cross the Gulf of Aden, where Sibu 1 was seized. Available data do not establish the effect of piracy on Ethiopian freight costs; this should be assessed when considering future maritime security arrangements. 5. The Federal Government's Case The Federal Government of Somalia presents its constitutional reforms as a step toward electoral and institutional change; questions concerning political consensus and security implications remain relevant. This brief does not assess their legal merits. The government says the amended constitution replaces clan-based power-sharing with one person, one vote, harmonizes state and federal electoral cycles, and was validly passed and signed on 8 March 2026, so the mandate runs to 2027. ²⁴ Voter registration is scheduled for 1-22 November 2026. ²⁵ Critics, including Puntland, Jubaland, former presidents and the Somali Future Council, say the changes lacked consensus and the required two-thirds majority. ²⁶ Parliament's four-year mandate ended in April 2026 without a transition plan. ²⁷ The sources reviewed do not show how a direct vote would work where Al-Shabaab holds or contests territory. Ethiopia has committed to work with the federal government and gains most from a Somalia able to sustain a joint front against Al-Shabaab. A contested political process may create security challenges regardless of its eventual outcome, so Ethiopia should support inclusive, AU or Turkey-facilitated dialogue over any position on who is right. 6. Recommendations • Work through established frameworks. Ethiopia should continue to act through the federal government of Somalia, the African Union and the Ankara process, and engage Somalia’s federal member states as complementary partners within the framework of AU principles. • Prioritize a post-2026 AUSSOM arrangement. Ethiopia should work with Mogadishu, the AU and its partners to secure a clear post-2026 arrangement for Ethiopian participation, in view of the reported 31 December 2026 deadline for the mandate and associated logistical support. • Strengthen border security with the Somali Regional State. Ethiopia should reinforce border defence and monitor the conditions that enabled the July 2022 incursion: control of border areas in Bakool and Gedo, the level of Ethiopian presence along the border, and competing military commitments elsewhere. • Assess maritime exposure before new agreements. Ethiopia should commission a risk assessment of piracy’s effect on freight costs and corridor reliability to inform consideration of future maritime or anti-piracy agreements. • Support inclusive political dialogue. Ethiopia should encourage AU- or Turkey-facilitated dialogue on Somalia’s electoral and constitutional process while respecting Somalia’s sovereignty and without taking a position on the legal merits, since a contested process is a security concern whichever side prevails. • Maintain a balanced approach and coordinate with other partners. Ethiopia should continue to maintain a balanced approach toward Mogadishu and the federal member states, and reassess it as developments unfold, including the potential deployment of Egyptian forces to Somalia under bilateral arrangements. somalia.summary: Ethiopia's strategic approach to Somalia's security transition beyond 2026 emphasizes collaboration with the Somali government, the African Union (AU), and the Ankara process, while enhancing its border security and evaluating maritime risks. The urgency stems from the impending expiration of the AU Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) on December 31, 2026, after which the U.S. will cease funding. Somalia's security has deteriorated due to internal disputes and setbacks against Al-Shabaab, which has regained territory despite previous gains by Somali forces. Ethiopia faces threats primarily from Al-Shabaab's incursions and piracy along the Puntland coast. To address these challenges, Ethiopia is advised to prioritize a post-2026 AUSSOM agreement, bolster border defenses, and support inclusive political dialogue in Somalia. Additionally, it should assess the implications of piracy on trade routes and maintain a balanced approach towards both the federal government and regional authorities to ensure stability in the Horn of Africa.

October 28, 2026 11 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s security sector costs more than $1 billion a year, but only a fraction of that sum passes through the government’s budget. The rest is paid by international partners, outside any consolidated fiscal account, leaving the state with limited visibility, weak control, and a mounting vulnerability as external support begins to contract. The figures, drawn from the World Bank’s 2026 Public Finance Review, reveal a security architecture that is expensive, fragmented, and structurally unsustainable. The review warns that the planned drawdown of the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia could force the government to assume costs it cannot afford, or preside over a decline in security capacity as external funding recedes. This picture is gloomier than the one FTL documented five years ago in “AMISOM: A Rescue Mission in Need of Rescue,” which traced how a mission originally scoped for 8,000 troops and six months grew into a 20,000-person operation spanning every federal member state. A Billion Dollars, Mostly Invisible Total security financing exceeds $1 billion annually, according to the World Bank. But less than 40 percent of that total is on-budget. The remainder comes through AUSSOM, the UN Support Office in Somalia, and bilateral arrangements with partner countries, none of which are fully reflected in the federal budget. That fragmentation has a history. The 2021 FTL Dhambaal reported that the original AMISOM cost estimate was $4 to $5 million. By 2021, the mission was costing $4 to $7 billion and counting, excluding bilateral support from the UK, the US, and the UN. Each successive UN Security Council resolution extended the mandate and expanded the objectives, adding reconciliation, political mediation, and a large civilian component that funded the AU Peace and Security Council in Addis Ababa. The Dhambaal described that body as functioning as a “retirement arrangement for AMISOM and AU staff,” allowing them to continue working on the EU budget while living in Addis Ababa or Nairobi. The 2026 federal budget allocated approximately $271 million to defence and national security. About $185 million went to defence and $86 million to national security, with the armed forces receiving roughly $177 million. These figures represent only a slice of the true cost of Somalia’s security apparatus. The external financing that fills the gap is increasingly uncertain. The UN Support Office has been operating on a depleted trust fund. By January 2026, support for rations and fuel had to be suspended, and only casualty and medical evacuation support remained. A small contribution in March allowed ration support to resume until April 30, but the trust fund was depleted again thereafter. Sustaining core activities across all mandated categories would require approximately $2.2 million per month, the UN Secretary-General reported in 2026. The Ghost Soldiers Problem Within the on-budget security spending, the payroll is the largest single component, and it is also the least verified. The Somali National Army’s payroll nearly doubled between 2020 and 2025, reaching approximately 47,438 personnel. But a 2025 verification exercise through the SNA ’s human resource management system found approximately 51,600 personnel in the force, of whom only 42,000 were active. The gap, roughly 9,600 personnel, represents close to one-fifth of the SNA payroll. These are individuals who are paid but not deployable. The World Bank describes the discrepancy as a failure of reconciliation between personnel records and payroll payments, with significant implications for fiscal leakage and operational readiness. This is not a new problem. The 2021 Dhambaal documented that troop-contributing countries had developed elaborate systems for deducting from soldiers’ allowances before they reached the individuals. Kenya was deducting $200 per soldier from the EU-funded allowances. Uganda and Burundi deducted the same amount. Djibouti kept $328. Ethiopia unilaterally decided to keep 50 percent of the allowances its soldiers earned serving in Somalia. The Kenyan Auditor-General at the time found that of the KShs.8.5 billion expected in EU reimbursements at the end of June 2019, only KShs.6.5 billion had reached the Treasury. The problem has now migrated to the Somali national payroll. In late October 2026, reports emerged that nearly 10,000 Somali soldiers had their salaries reduced as part of a military personnel verification process known as suul-saar (finger print) , intended to establish who is eligible to receive salaries. Some personnel also received outstanding entitlements unpaid since 2024. The Ministry of Defence has not provided a detailed public explanation of the deductions, the number affected, or the procedures available for complaints. The World Bank recommends continuous biometric payroll verification for the security sector, integrated with the government’s financial management and human resource systems, to establish a credible staffing baseline and eliminate unverified personnel. The 2021 Dhambaal noted, bluntly, that “the Somali Security Apparatus is aggressively against any monitoring mission as relates to the actual SNA numbers and utilization of resources.” Wages, Not Warfare Even where personnel are verified and paid, the composition of security spending undermines effectiveness. The World Bank found that spending is heavily skewed toward salaries and allowances, with limited investment in operational and capital inputs. Since 2020, spending increases have been driven primarily by salaries, allowances, and food and catering. Non-wage operational spending, including fuel, maintenance, training, and communications, has not kept pace with personnel growth. Capital and equipment spending remains negligible and largely externally financed. The result, the World Bank concludes, is a “high cost, low capability” model in which higher staffing does not translate into improved operational effectiveness. Each dollar of the wage bill financing inactive personnel or unconsolidated allowances is a dollar unavailable for either operational readiness or civilian priorities. The 2021 Dhambaal documented a similar dynamic in the AU mission. The mission had expanded “far beyond the agreed strategic locations in Mogadishu” to cover almost all federal member states, with more than 20,000 troops on the ground instead of the initial 8,000. The original idea of transitioning AMISOM into a UN peacekeeping operation was “abandoned and actively undermined by AU members who overtly benefit from a protracted AU mission and the status quo, both financially and politically.” The AUSSOM Cliff The most immediate risk is the transition from AUSSOM, and the specific terms of that transition are now becoming clear. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Washington’s position on UNSOS , the United States has proposed a 12-month drawdown of UNSOS followed immediately by liquidation, after the current AUSSOM authorisation expires on December 31, 2026. That proposal falls short of what Somalia, the African Union, and troop-contributing countries had sought. At the second extraordinary summit of troop-contributing countries in Kampala on July 31, 2026, representatives from Uganda, Kenya, Burundi, Ethiopia, Egypt, and Djibouti appealed for 18 to 24 months of continued UN support to enable the implementation of agreed milestones and the orderly transfer of security responsibilities. Washington rejected the extension. The financial stakes are significant: the UN General Assembly has approved an appropriation of $481 million for UNSOS for the current financial year, with the US providing approximately 26 percent through assessed contributions. AUSSOM, which fields nearly 12,000 personnel, relies on UNSOS for about 85 percent of its support requirements, including food, water, fuel, medical services, and troop transportation. AUSSOM Commander Lt Gen Sam Kavuma has warned that if UNSOS support ends, it could significantly affect the mission’s capabilities. The UN support office has already begun preparing for liquidation. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the UNSOS disposal process , the mission has issued a public tender seeking qualified auctioneers to sell a wide range of UN-owned equipment and vehicles, including generators, medical and laboratory equipment, prefabricated accommodation materials, and heavy construction machinery, valued at approximately $30 million. The National Security Adviser and the AUSSOM chief met at Villa Somalia in October to discuss the transition, with the government stating it is ready to take over responsibility. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the transition talks , the plan envisions a phased transfer of duties, but the financial underpinnings remain precarious. The closure of the UN political mission, UNTMIS, on October 31 adds another layer of uncertainty. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the UNTMIS closure , the mission’s mandated functions have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, but the political good offices that UNTMIS provided will not be easily replaced. The Dhambaal’s account of the AU’s manoeuvring in 2021 remains relevant. When the UN Independent Assessment recommended a reconfigured AMISOM that would support Somali forces rather than lead security efforts, the AU commissioned its own “independent” assessment, which recommended a hybrid AU-UN multidimensional stabilization mission covering 2022 to 2026. The AU then organized an ad hoc meeting with the Somali government and convinced two ministries, Justice and Defence, to sign an agreement that the Foreign Ministry had not been consulted on. The FGS rejected the hybrid option five days after the AU Peace and Security Council endorsed it. The episode illustrated, as the Dhambaal put it, that “the ‘African solutions to African problems’ narrative is crippled.” The Fiscal Arithmetic Somalia’s ability to absorb additional security costs is constrained by its domestic revenue base. Domestic revenue reached an estimated 6.3 percent of GDP in 2025, a level the World Bank describes as insufficient to finance core state functions and development needs, let alone a security sector currently sustained by external partners. The government’s 2027 draft budget is 9.2 percent smaller than the 2026 budget, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Cabinet-approved draft . A smaller budget, combined with a security transition that will require Somalia to assume costs currently borne by international partners, creates a fiscal squeeze that the World Bank has explicitly warned against. The Bank’s recommendation is to shift from headcount-based budgeting to capability-based security planning that accounts for the full cost of operational readiness, including equipment, maintenance, logistics, and training. It also calls for a joint, costed transition plan with AUSSOM and key partners, grounded in realistic domestic financing capacity and an affordable force structure. Critical Note The World Bank’s findings describe a security sector that is expensive but not efficient, large but not capable, and dependent but not sustainable. The 2021 FTL Dhambaal reached the same conclusion about AMISOM: a mission that was supposed to rescue the Somali government had itself become a rescue mission in need of rescue. The $1 billion annual price tag is real, but it is paid largely by others. The 9,600 non-active personnel on the SNA payroll are a symptom of a deeper problem: a state that cannot yet verify, control, or afford its own forces. The US proposal for a 12-month UNSOS drawdown is a pragmatic compromise that recognises the logistical realities of winding down a mission as complex as UNSOS. A rapid liquidation would leave AUSSOM without critical support before alternative arrangements are in place. The tender for auctioneers to dispose of $30 million in equipment shows that the drawdown is already underway, whether or not the political arrangements are finalized. The reported salary deductions affecting nearly 10,000 soldiers are a reminder that the fiscal crisis is not abstract. It is measured in the unpaid wages of men who are expected to fight. The government’s failure to explain the deductions publicly, or to provide a clear appeals process, compounds the grievance. A soldier who cannot trust his pay is a soldier whose loyalty is uncertain. The AUSSOM transition is the central test. The international community has funded Somalia’s security for nearly two decades. That funding is now contracting, and the government has not yet demonstrated that it can replace it. The closure of UNTMIS removes one more layer of international political support at precisely the moment when Somalia needs it most. The World Bank’s recommendations are sound: biometric verification, capability-based budgeting, a costed transition plan. But they require political will that has been in short supply. As the Dhambaal warned in 2021, the donors have an opportunity to learn from Afghanistan and push for a situation in which the Somali government takes full responsibility for its own security. Whether they will seize that opportunity, or preside over another unfinished transition, is the question that the 2027 budget review will begin to answer.
